theory.intro: A **conditional probability** is the probability of one event happening **given that** another event has already happened. Knowing that event $B$ has happened rules out every outcome outside $B$, so the sample space is **reduced** to $B$ alone. The probability is written $P(A \mid B)$, read '$A$ given $B$', and is found by counting the favourable outcomes **inside the reduced sample space**.
facts: $P(A \mid B)$ is read 'the probability of $A$ given $B$' — the probability that $A$ happens knowing that $B$ has happened.
The phrases '**given that**', '**if** … **then**', '**of**' and '**knowing that**' all signal a condition, and the event named by the condition goes **after** the bar.
The condition **reduces the sample space**: only the outcomes in $B$ are still possible, so $n(B)$ replaces the total as the denominator.
Counting elements, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(B)}$; working from probabilities, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$.
The numerator is $n(A \cap B)$, not $n(A)$ — an outcome must be in $A$ **and** still lie inside the reduced sample space.

$P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ are **different**: they have different denominators, so swapping the event and the condition usually changes the answer. This is the most common mistake with conditional language.
When $A$ and $B$ are **dependent**, knowing $B$ changes how likely $A$ is. When they are **independent** it does not, so $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
Give a probability as a fraction in simplest form, unless the data are decimals or percentages, in which case keep that form.
steps: Reduce the sample space to the condition.
Count the favourable outcomes inside it.

foundation.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed at a school canteen on one day.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Year 10} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 18 & 9 & 27 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 12 & 21 & 33 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 30 & 30 & 60 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random. Find the probability that it is hot food, given that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the Year $9$ column, which has a total of $30$ orders.
Of those $30$ orders, $18$ are hot food.
$P(\text{hot food} \mid \text{Year } 9) = \frac{18}{30}$
$= \frac{3}{5}$

foundation.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed at a school canteen on one day.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Year 10} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 18 & 9 & 27 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 12 & 21 & 33 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 30 & 30 & 60 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random. Find the probability that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, given that it is hot food, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
Now the condition restricts the sample space to the hot food row, which has a total of $27$ orders.
Of those $27$ orders, $18$ came from Year $9$.
$P(\text{Year } 9 \mid \text{hot food}) = \frac{18}{27}$
$= \frac{2}{3}$

foundation.question_text:
Let $B$ be the event 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ be the event 'a student has a part-time job'. Write each statement using conditional probability notation.
a. The probability that a student has a part-time job, **given that** they catch the bus.
b. **If** a student has a part-time job, **then** the probability that they catch the bus.
foundation.solution_text:
a. 'Given that they catch the bus' names the condition, so $B$ goes after the bar.
$P(J \mid B)$
b. 'If a student has a part-time job' names the condition, so $J$ goes after the bar.
$P(B \mid J)$

foundation.question_text:
Let $L$ be the event 'a student is left-handed' and $C$ be the event 'a student buys lunch at the canteen'. Write each statement using conditional probability notation.
a. The probability that a student is left-handed, **knowing that** they buy lunch at the canteen.
b. $18\%$ **of** the students who are left-handed buy lunch at the canteen.
foundation.solution_text:
a. 'Knowing that they buy lunch at the canteen' names the condition, so $C$ goes after the bar.
$P(L \mid C)$
b. 'Of the students who are left-handed' names the group the percentage is taken from, so $L$ is the condition.
$P(C \mid L) = 18\%$

foundation.question_text: In a class of $30$ students, $18$ have a part-time job, $12$ catch the bus to school and $8$ both have a part-time job and catch the bus. One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student has a part-time job, given that they catch the bus, as a fraction in simplest form.

At a large school, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.15$, where $B$ is the event 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is the event 'a student has a part-time job'. Find $P(J \mid B)$ as a decimal.

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows how $60$ students travel to school and whether they have a part-time job.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Job} & \text{No job} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Catches bus} & 14 & 22 & 36 \\ \text{Walks} & 6 & 18 & 24 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 20 & 40 & 60 \end{array}$
One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student catches the bus, given that they do not have a part-time job, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the 'No job' column, whose total is $40$.
Of those $40$ students, $22$ catch the bus.
$P(\text{bus} \mid \text{no job}) = \frac{22}{40}$
$= \frac{11}{20}$

development.question_text: At a large school, $30\%$ of students are left-handed. Being left-handed is independent of whether a student catches the bus to school. Find $P(L \mid B)$ as a percentage, where $L$ is 'the student is left-handed' and $B$ is 'the student catches the bus', and explain your answer.
development.solution_text:
The two events are independent, so knowing that a student catches the bus gives no new information about whether they are left-handed.
The reduced sample space of bus catchers has the same proportion of left-handed students as the whole school.
$P(L \mid B) = P(L)$
$= 30\%$

development.question_text: In a survey of $40$ students, $16$ have a part-time job, $24$ catch the bus to school and $12$ both have a part-time job and catch the bus. Show that having a part-time job and catching the bus are dependent events for this group, by comparing $P(J)$ with $P(J \mid B)$.

A researcher surveys students about travelling to school and part-time work. Which of these two questions is asking for a conditional probability, and which is not? Write each one in probability notation, using $B$ for 'catches the bus' and $J$ for 'has a part-time job'.
a. A student is chosen at random from the whole survey. What is the probability that they catch the bus and have a part-time job?
b. A student is chosen at random from those who catch the bus. What is the probability that they have a part-time job?
development.solution_text:
a. The student is chosen from the whole survey, so the sample space is not reduced and both events must happen.
$P(B \cap J)$
This is not a conditional probability.
b. The student is chosen only from the bus catchers, so the sample space has been reduced to $B$ before the choice is made.
$P(J \mid B)$
This is the conditional probability.

development.question_text: At a large school, $P(B) = 0.45$, $P(J) = 0.2$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.12$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'. Find $P(B \mid J)$ as a decimal.
development.solution_text:
The condition is $J$, so the denominator is $P(J)$, not $P(B)$.
$P(B \mid J) = \frac{P(J \cap B)}{P(J)}$
$= \frac{0.12}{0.2}$
$= 0.6$

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed by $80$ students at a school canteen.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 8} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 15 & 21 & 36 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 25 & 19 & 44 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 40 & 40 & 80 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random. Find the probability that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, given that it is a sandwich, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the sandwich row, whose total is $44$.
Of those $44$ orders, $19$ came from Year $9$.
$P(\text{Year } 9 \mid \text{sandwich}) = \frac{19}{44}$

mastery.question_text:
The two-way table shows a survey of $80$ students.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Bus} & \text{No bus} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Job} & 18 & 6 & 24 \\ \hline \text{No job} & 42 & 14 & 56 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 60 & 20 & 80 \end{array}$
A newsletter claims: 'Most students with a part-time job catch the bus, so most students who catch the bus have a part-time job.' Test both halves of the claim by calculating the relevant conditional probabilities as fractions in simplest form, and state whether the claim is valid.
mastery.solution_text:
1. **Reduce the sample space to the condition**
For the first half the condition is 'has a part-time job', giving a reduced sample space of $24$ students.
For the second half the condition is 'catches the bus', giving a reduced sample space of $60$ students.
2. **Count the favourable outcomes inside it**
Both halves count the same $18$ students in the top-left cell.
3. **Write the fraction and simplify**
$P(\text{bus} \mid \text{job}) = \frac{18}{24}$
$= \frac{3}{4}$
$P(\text{job} \mid \text{bus}) = \frac{18}{60}$
$= \frac{3}{10}$
Three quarters of the job holders do catch the bus, so the first half is correct.
Only $\frac{3}{10}$ of the bus catchers have a job, so the second half is false and the claim is not valid — reversing the condition changes the denominator from $24$ to $60$.

mastery.question_text: At a large school, $P(B) = 0.6$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.15$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'. Find $P(J' \mid B)$ as a decimal.
mastery.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the denominator is $P(B) = 0.6$.
Inside $B$, the favourable students are those without a part-time job, so subtract the overlap from $P(B)$.
$P(J' \cap B) = 0.6 - 0.15$
$= 0.45$
$P(J' \mid B) = \frac{0.45}{0.6}$
$= 0.75$
